8bd9b4222003e66a: Microsoft is pushing its data analytics and engineering environment to a new set of commercial users that are an “order of magnitude” greater than its current base. Power BI has become a popular biz intelligence system - with more than 425,000 customers worldwide - particularly among customers of the Microsoft Dynamics application portfolio. Now, Microsoft execs are trying to exploit this penetration by offering Power BI customers high-end database services and app building tools available on its Fabric data analytics and engineering platform. Customers who license Power BI Pro and Power BI Premium Per User will get Fabric Apps and Fabric Database capabilities (up to 1GB per app), along with security, at no additional cost. Microsoft argues that the Apps customers are building in Fabric can be ported to Power BI without much additional work or cost. Arun Ulag, exec veep at Microsoft, told The Register: “We have 40,000 Fabric customers today. Power BI is an order of magnitude larger, with 425,000 customers: organizations, not individuals. The usage of Power BI exceeds 35 million business users every month,” he said. Microsoft is now offering this user base the ability to build data analytics-style apps using Rayfin, an open source SDK. The company says Rafin will let users create their own data applications that accept inputs, write back data, preserve shared state, and support operational workflows across to Fabric. Each application gets a 1GB Fabric SQL database, authentication, and security. As an application grows, users can expand its functionality and hand it off to developers and IT teams without rebuilding it. By bringing Fabric application development to Power BI, Microsoft is showing that the “distinctions between a dashboard and an app are disappearing,” Ulag said. Rayfin is designed to work with GitHub Copilot; Claude Code or Codex; or any coding agent, letting users instruct a coding agent to build an application and deploy where they specify, in a Fabric environment.The feature is scheduled to be available in preview in the coming weeks. Fabric was anounced by Microsoft in 2023 as an integrated analytics, data warehouse and data lake environment. It has since added data mirroring to allow users to run analytics on data in other environments without pushing SQL queries directly to them. Last year, the vendor added transactional databases to the environment, including its document database Cosmos DB and Fabric SQL relational system. Microsoft says it is now extending its integration with other platforms, including Salesforce application and data systems. It is previewing bidirectional integration with Salesforce Data Cloud 360, making data from the CRM vendor available across the Microsoft system for analytics and AI, including as business context for Fabric data agents, without duplicating that data. Salesforce also has its own data environment and agent-building platform.®
72a60e46787a21bc: GENEVA, Sept 29 — The UN voiced worry today as Malaysia started sending thousands of Myanmar nationals back to the war-torn country, warning that conditions there would not enable “safe, dignified and sustainable returns”.
Malaysia began repatriating around 1,500 Myanmar nationals today, launching the first phase of a return programme that has raised concerns from rights groups.
The group is the first of 5,000 Myanmar nationals that Malaysia says have agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres.
“We are concerned,” United Nations refugee agency spokesman Matthew Saltmarsh told reporters in Geneva.

“With ongoing armed conflict and widespread violence and human rights violations across Myanmar, UNHCR maintains that current conditions do not permit safe, dignified and sustainable returns,” he said.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced in July that Myanmar had agreed to take back 5,000 members of its persecuted Rohingya minority, in a rare repatriation push that has prompted concern from rights groups.
Myanmar earlier this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the UN and rights groups.
It was not immediately clear on Tuesday how many in the first group en route to Myanmar were Rohingya, and Malaysian authorities did not divulge the number.
But the Muslim minority makes up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in the country, according to the UN.
“Under international law, no one should be sent to a country where they may face persecution, torture, serious harm or other threats to life, liberty and security,” Saltmarsh insisted. — AFP
5958f3948e2f779f: SINGAPORE, Sept 29 — Singapore Airlines (SIA) said today it will unveil an upgraded travel experience in Singapore in November, with changes to in-flight dining the first to be announced.
The Singapore carrier said the upgrade will cover new cabin products, the KrisWorld entertainment system, amenities, high-speed connectivity and ground services.
It gave no details on those other areas in its press release.
On dining, SIA said it is introducing more than 100 new and revised appetisers, main courses and desserts across all cabin classes.
The dishes fall under a new menu category called SIA Chefs’ Selection, developed by the airline’s in-house and guest chefs with its catering partners.
SIA said it has begun rolling out the new dishes progressively.
The remaining dining changes will be introduced from November.
Passengers in Suites, First Class and Business Class will get new wine labels, while new spirits will be offered in all cabins.
A selection of appetisers, main courses, and desserts for First Class and Business Class passengers in SIA’s revamped inflight dining from November 2026. — Picture courtesy of Singapore Airlines
Meals in those three cabins will be served on tableware made with French luxury house Christofle, incorporating a subtle version of SIA’s batik motif.
In Suites and First Class, selected dishes will be presented with “distinctive touches”, and cabin crew may recommend drinks to go with meals.
SIA senior vice-president for customer experience Yeoh Phee Teik said in-flight dining is “about much more than the meal itself”.
He said the airline reviewed everything from menu design to crew service, guided by customer feedback and dining trends.
The statement did not name specific dishes, wines or routes.
bbeb316536e7f2a9: JAKARTA, Sept 29 — Indonesian police charged a train driver Tuesday with allegedly failing to hit the brakes in time to prevent a crash that killed 16 women near Jakarta in April, an official said.
A long-distance train smashed on April 28 into a women-only car at the back of a stationary commuter train near Bekasi Timur station outside the capital.
Rescuers worked for hours into the night to pry open the crumpled carriages.
The 37-year-old driver of the long-distance train now faces multiple charges after an investigation found he had hit the brakes too close to the stalled commuter train.
“Investigators concluded that the emergency braking action could have been carried out further away,” Jakarta police official I Dewa Putu Gede Anom Danujaya told a press conference.
The driver risks up to 12 years in prison if found guilty, said Dewa.
The incident killed 16 passengers of the women-only carriage — a feature on Indonesian trains to shield women from sexual harassment while commuting.
Another 107 people were injured, according to a National Transportation Safety Committee (KNKT) report.
The report said several factors, including signalling and communication system failures, contributed to the crash.
The train driver is not under arrest.
Transport accidents are common in Indonesia, a vast archipelago nation where buses, trains and ships are often old and poorly maintained. — AFP
fe5c62977a8f429e: Airport departure boards are supposed to tell passengers where and when their flights will leave. Recent examples spotted by eagle-eyed Reg readers have offered some bonus information: a Windows activation reminder, dates from the past, and a glimpse of what appears to be Windows 7 beneath the signage software. Airport borks, it seems, are like buses: three have arrived in quick succession at Heathrow. The first display shows a Windows activation watermark behind a list of departures to glamorous destinations. Milan? How lovely. Cairo? A place to ponder culture and millennia-old construction techniques. Activate Windows? OK, not quite so lovely. Perhaps the destination board had simply embarked on a journey of self-discovery. But at least the date was correct, right? Er, wrong. Time might be moving forward for the rest of the world, but at Heathrow it appears to be going backward. Perhaps heading to a time when air traffic control wasn't beset by problems and air travel didn't involve increasingly performative security protocols that differ country by country. Our second serving of signage silage shows one page dated September 21 and another stuck on September 12. A number switcheroo? A window into the past? Or simply a display that had stopped receiving updates? Alas, things became more unsettling a few days later when another Heathrow screen revealed the eldritch horror lurking beneath the departures display. Is that... Windows 7? The network dialog looks an awful lot like something from the operating system that refuses to die. The taskbar and Start button peeking out from the bottom of the screen only deepen the suspicion. Then again, Heathrow is no stranger to displaying retired technology. A British Airways Concorde remains parked at the airport, reminding passengers stuffed into yet another Boeing or Airbus that air travel was once considerably more ambitious – and perhaps a little more dangerous. When Concorde retired in 2003, Microsoft was two years into the Windows XP era. A different sort of danger, perhaps, but at least nobody had yet asked it to run an airport departures board in 2026. ®
5f9e882e9b0d7f81: PUTRAJAYA, Sept 29 — S&P Global Ratings has reaffirmed Malaysia’s sovereign credit rating at ‘A-’ with a Stable outlook, citing the economy’s resilience and diversification, sustained growth momentum and continued fiscal consolidation.

The ratings agency expects Malaysia’s economy to expand 5.5 per cent in 2026, following 5.2 per cent growth in 2025 and 5.7 per cent year-on-year growth in the first half of 2026, the Ministry of Finance said.

S&P forecasts average annual growth of five per cent between 2026 and 2029, while Malaysia’s 10-year weighted-average real GDP per capita growth is estimated at 3.7 per cent, above the global median for peers at similar income levels.

Prime Minister and Finance Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the assessment reflected the government’s efforts under the Ekonomi Madani framework to strengthen fiscal foundations while sustaining growth and protecting the rakyat from external volatility.
“S&P’s assessment that Malaysia’s 10-year weighted-average real GDP per capita growth remains above the global median for peers at similar income levels is encouraging.

“It shows that growth per person has remained strong, while we have continued to protect the rakyat from the impact of external inflationary pressures despite an increasingly challenging global environment,” he added.

S&P attributed the reaffirmation partly to stronger electrical and electronics and semiconductor shipments linked to the global artificial intelligence investment cycle, higher energy exports and buoyant household consumption.
It said Malaysia’s established E&E ecosystem, together with initiatives such as the Ekonomi Madani framework and New Industrial Master Plan 2030, could support longer-term economic expansion.

The agency also noted that Malaysia had emerged as South-east Asia’s leading data-centre investment destination, attracting an estimated RM386 billion in cumulative investment between 2021 and mid-2026.
On fiscal management, S&P recognised Malaysia’s sustained consolidation, with the fiscal deficit narrowing from 6.4 per cent of GDP in 2021 to 3.7 per cent in 2025.

The Public Finance and Fiscal Responsibility Act 2023 was also highlighted as providing a framework for stronger fiscal governance, transparency and risk management, with S&P noting that the legislation has bipartisan support and will guide the country’s medium-term fiscal framework.

Malaysia’s external position remains a source of resilience, supported by its large and diversified export base and a track record of current account surpluses spanning more than two decades, with S&P expecting the surplus to stabilise at around 1.8 per cent of GDP over the next three years.
S&P also assessed Bank Negara Malaysia as having significant independence and strong monetary policy credibility, with inflation expectations remaining well anchored.
Anwar said the government would continue advancing reforms under Ekonomi Madani and the Thirteenth Malaysia Plan 2026-2030, focusing on fiscal sustainability, productivity and competitiveness.
“Our task now is to ensure that stronger growth translates more meaningfully into higher incomes, better opportunities and improved living standards for the rakyat.
“Belanjawan 2027, to be tabled on 9 October 2026, will build on these reforms with further measures to achieve that objective,” he said.
0b5586d14cc1d517: SEPANG, Sept 29 — A special fly-past will be held in conjunction with the Formula 1 (F1) Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix (GP) at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC) on Sunday (October 4), according to the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM).
CAAM deputy chief executive officer (Air Navigation Services) Zainul Abidin Maslan said the air show, to be managed by Gulf Air, would be held tomorrow for the rehearsal and on race day.
He said CAAM had made technical and service preparations to ensure the performance runs smoothly.
"There will be a low fly-past by Gulf Air just as the race takes off. That one has been coordinated with our team, both control centres and the KLIA control tower.

“It will cause very minimum disruption to air traffic. We are also ready to accommodate that kind of operation during race day,” he said during the CAAM-Media Literacy Programme question-and-answer session here today.
Also present were CAAM chairman Datuk Mohamed Sharil Tarmizi and Malaysian Press Institute (MPI) president Datuk Yong Soo Heong.

Meanwhile, Zainul Abidin said CAAM is ready to accommodate additional flights transporting F1 team logistics, while also ensuring that the fly-past operation does not disrupt the smooth flow of air traffic on race day.
He added that air traffic volume on that day is expected to remain normal, with only a few additional flights transporting logistics for the teams participating in the race.
Malaysia is set to welcome F1 back to the SIC after nine years, through the hosting of the F1 Bahrain GP from October 2-4.
The SIC previously hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017, before it was dropped from the F1 calendar following rising hosting costs and licensing fees.
The prestigious race's return to Malaysia follows successful diplomacy between His Majesty Sultan Ibrahim, King of Malaysia, and King Hamad Isa Al-Khalifa of Bahrain. — Bernama
ee50c82d2f789696: TOKYO, Sept 29 — Japanese volleyball player Rui Takahashi came out as gay on Tuesday, saying he wanted to help others struggling with their sexuality in a country where openly LGBTQ athletes are extremely rare.
The 26-year-old Takahashi, who plays in the top division of Japan’s professional volleyball league, posted a statement on social media accompanied by a black-and-white photo of himself.
In it, he said he had been “afraid to face a certain side of myself” since he was young.
“I struggled with it and ended up denying who I was,” he wrote.
“That is the fact that I am gay and that I am one of the sexual minorities.”
Takahashi said his brother Ran, who is a hugely popular star with Japan’s national volleyball team, helped him come to terms with his sexuality.
“Talking with Ran became the trigger that finally allowed me to accept myself for the first time,” he wrote.
“By putting my feelings into words, I was able to sort out my thoughts, and little by little I started to feel that it was OK to be just the way I am.”
Takahashi becomes one of a very small group of openly LGBTQ professional athletes in Japan.
Women’s football player Shiho Shimoyamada was the first to come out as gay in 2019.
Kumi Yokoyama, who played for Japan at the Women’s World Cup, later came out as a transgender man.
In June 2021, the Japanese Olympic Committee appointed transgender former fencer Fumino Suhiyama to its board of directors, just weeks before the Tokyo Olympics.
Takahashi said he hoped him coming out would help others in a similar situation.
“I would be happy if my decision to face myself and speak in my own words could, even in a small way, become a catalyst for them,” he wrote. — AFP
d2510b3d9a1cdb9d: SEPANG, Sept 29 — Formula One’s return to the Sepang International Circuit (SIC) after a nine-year absence is set to offer drivers with a fresh challenge and fans with a potentially unpredictable race as the Formula 1 (F1) Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix gets underway this weekend.

Bahrain Motor Federation (BMF) General Manager Abdulaziz Al Thawadi said Sepang’s demanding layout and changeable weather could make the October 2-4 race particularly interesting for drivers, especially those with no previous Formula One experience at the Malaysian circuit.

“It should not be difficult for them, but it will be something new, a different layout. The drivers will always love to have a different layout, a different circuit, a different challenge,” he told Bernama here on Tuesday.
Al Thawadi said drivers unfamiliar with Sepang could prepare through simulators, while the circuit’s weather conditions could force teams to adapt their strategies throughout the weekend.
“Here, yes. We do remember some races here; they have very heavy rain. So yes, here we cannot predict anything.
“I mean, look at today’s weather. Yesterday was sunny; today it is foggy. Every day is a different thing.
“So that is a good thing, actually. It is good for the drivers; it is a good challenge. They change their strategy, and it will become more interesting,” he said.
He described Sepang as one of the best circuits in terms of layout and track characteristics adding that feedback from Formula One teams had been positive.
Al Thawadi said a 522-member BMF contingent comprising race officials, administrative personnel and marshals had been deployed for the event.
They are supported by around 300 Malaysian marshals, as well as local medical, civil defence and other support personnel, bringing the overall workforce to nearly 1,000.
Formula One last raced at Sepang in 2017, when Max Verstappen won the Malaysian Grand Prix.
The circuit hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017 before dropping off the Formula One calendar.

This weekend’s race marks Formula One’s return to Sepang after nine years, with the Bahrain Grand Prix relocated to Malaysia after the original April event in Sakhir was cancelled amid the situation in West Asia. — Bernama
cddb71b45869b959: BUTTERWORTH, Sept 29 —The Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development (KPWKM) is calling on students to know their boundaries, dare to say no, and seek help if they face sexual harassment or violence.
Deputy Minister Lim Hui Ying said this awareness is crucial to keeping schools a safe environment for children.

Beyond victims coming forward, she said, friends and family members must also play their part by offering support if they notice behavioural changes or suspicious circumstances among those close to them.
“If they feel they cannot accept it, they must dare to say no. We also want to teach them how to seek help when someone faces sexual harassment or violence.

“This is not a case or situation to be ashamed of. They must dare to come forward and look for channels of help,” she told reporters after the Zero Tolerance for Violence: Respect the Boundaries programme at Sekolah Menengah Jenis Kebangsaan Chung Ling here today.
Lim said bullying, sexual harassment and violence require a cross-ministry approach, covering advocacy, prevention, awareness and counselling.
She said KPWKM, through the Social Welfare Department, also has professional counsellors who can assist schools if needed.
Meanwhile, Lim said 142 complaints had been filed with the Tribunal for Anti-Sexual Harassment (TAGS) as of Sept 20, with 97 of them successfully resolved.

e288e89c8be6b663: EVENT: Somewhere in your organisation right now, somebody is trying to work out which of four copies of a file is the current one. They will probably get it right, after twenty minutes and a message to a colleague in another time zone, and nobody will log the twenty minutes. That is what it costs to run distributed teams on file infrastructure built for an office, and most organisations have stopped noticing. The NAS is still there. So is the VPN, and so is the habit of downloading a file to work on it and syncing it back later, which arrived with the first remote worker and never left. None of it fails outright. The bill turns up somewhere else, as duplicated storage, as time spent waiting, and as a security review that finds one file in three places with three different sets of permissions. The Register is putting that problem to a dinner in Soho on Tuesday 20 October. Joe Fay of The Register chairs. Rupert Watson, VP GTM for EMEA at LucidLink, joins the conversation. It runs under the Chatham House Rule, so what is said can be used and who said it cannot, and the chair’s job includes stopping anyone who starts to pitch. What makes an evening like this useful is the detail people only share in private. The workaround a team adopted the week the office emptied and has been paying for ever since, for instance, and what they did about it once somebody added up the cost. Nobody says that on a recorded webinar. The questions for the table: how organisations are handling the growth in unstructured data, how they support distributed teams without paying for the same file three times, what they are doing about sync and version control, and whether any of it holds up in a security incident. Nobody is proposing to rip the estate out. The evening is about modernising around the storage and governance investments already made. The table is for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders carrying this now. Dinner runs from 6.30pm to 9pm at The Soho Hotel. Places are limited and go by invitation. Request one here.

540baec4726ad2a4: The World Wide Web’s decades-long tyranny of box design is finally coming to an end. A new set of CSS features – including the shape() function, and the border-shape and corner-shape properties – offers web designers and their AI agents a broader palette for laying out content in a more fluid manner. When the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) published its first standard for web page layout in 1996, web sites emulated the grid-defined layouts of academic papers, newspapers, and magazines. At the time, graphics drivers, and browser rendering engines were all in a relatively primitive state. Developers were also trying to grapple with a new medium and generally found that flowing text within a defined space was much easier when the geometric coordinates of that space were kept as simple as possible. But now print is basically dead, webdevs are savvier (and if not, AI is happy to help), and Lord knows GPUs are more powerful. So there's no reason today why a web page has to be square, daddy-o. In Edwin A. Abbott's 1884 proto-Sci-Fi classic Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions, the protagonist who lives in flat two-dimensional space is abruptly exposed to the dizzying world of three dimensions, much to his astonishment. Web developers may experience similar emotions when they first use these new CSS constructs. Dev’s choice: vertical or horizontal In their original forms, HTML and CSS could draw only horizontal or vertical lines or borders on a Web page. Fancier layouts required proprietary plug-ins, such as Java Applets, Macromedia/Adobe Flash, or some tedious JavaScript hacks. SVG first broke the boxiness of the web, giving the developers the ability to put curves, squiggly lines, logos or any other wild-ass shape desired by using a series of numerical coordinates to describe the shape (it’s tedious work, though image-to-SVG converters help). SVG was limited to a canvas placed on a Web page, however. CSS ruled the layout of the page itself. The first attempt at bridging the two worlds was path(), which allowed SVG to be embedded directly within CSS. The path() function had some limitations – it wasn’t responsive to changing web page sizes and it didn’t understand variables or CSS units of measurement. Developers had to define all specs in pixels and that was that. Check out those curves The shape() function properly introduced the Web to richer design. A shape() is a set of geometric coordinates of a desired shape or trajectory. Unlike path()’s reliance on SVG, it is built on responsive CSS syntax. When combined with the existing clip-path property, shape() has been used to create ticket stubs, chat bubbles, and other assorted page flotsam. The latest CSS property, border-shape, completes the work by applying CSS-native coordinates defined in shape() to the web page borders themselves. Define the coordinates with shape(), embed it in a border-shape property, and the boundaries are staked out on the page itself. The boundaries are laid out early in the rendering process, rather than clipped in near the end of the rendering. “In other words, putting borders on CSS shapes will become child’s play!” noted self-described CSS hacker Temani Afif, in a tutorial on the CSS-Tricks site. This new property opens a range of design possibilities heretofore too complicated to contemplate – at least within a 40-hour webdev workweek. Afif offers a number of demonstrations in his tutorials: not only can you carve up a Web page any way you see fit, but you can also put borders within borders. Fill in the space between the outer shape and the inner shape to make a cut-out. Shape an open heart inside a square box, for instance, using nothing but CSS. Either the outside border or the internal shape can be animated, allowing the outside border to change shape as the mouse goes over it, or the inside border to be filled with an image or another design. A shape can enlarge or shrink when the mouse hovers over it, or text can be highlighted with little squiggly lines. If hand-crafting the contents of shape() is not your jam, a companion property called corner-shape offers a number of pre-defined fancy border patterns. Most are variations of the standard box, including boxes with rounded edges, beveled edges, notches, scoops, and one called a “squircle.” According to the caniuse.com site, all major browsers now support shape(), while border-shape and corner-shape are still being implemented and considered experimental (though the current releases of Chrome, Edge, and Opera support the standard). Now, it’s up to developers to build a more fluid web. ®

7912342139f3efcb: AI tools are increasingly replacing human judgements in some settings. For instance, resume screening algorithms are often used in hiring, where they may improve efficiency and consistency in decision-making. But some scholars have raised concerns that the adoption of automated systems could eventually result in one algorithm being used to make all decisions in a particular industry. They worry so-called algorithmic monoculture could have negative consequences. For example, in hiring, the thinking goes that algorithmic monoculture might result in systematic exclusion — a situation in which a job candidate rejected by one firm’s algorithm would likely also be rejected by every other firm’s algorithm. However, MIT researchers now argue that algorithmic monoculture may not always be as bad as some scientists have suggested. They systematically evaluated major objections to algorithmic monoculture, including systematic exclusion, and concluded this and many other arguments either fail or aren’t decisive against all forms of monoculture.  Instead, they mathematically prove that monoculture tends to create informational echo chambers that can hinder exploration. In hiring, this could make it less likely that the best candidates would get jobs — however, bundling various hiring algorithms into a single “ensemble” can overcome this limitation, the researchers show. This could sometimes enable monoculture to perform as well as, if not better than, a polyculture where different firms use different algorithms. “A trend toward algorithmic monoculture is a realistic scenario, and a really important issue that is being brought about by the use of AI, but it is hard to say in the abstract whether monoculture would be a bad thing. It depends on the details, like the domain we are talking about and the accuracy of the algorithm itself,” says study co-author Brian Hedden, a professor in the Department of Linguistics and Philosophy, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and is also a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). Hedden is joined on the paper by co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management and in EECS, as well as a LIDS principal investigator. The research appears in Philosophical Perspectives.  The move toward monoculture Algorithmic monoculture, in which all decisions across a certain domain are made using the same algorithm, is not a new phenomenon.  For instance, lending decisions were once made by independent bankers at individual banks, but now all bankers use the same information based on a borrower’s standardized credit scores, which are derived from the Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) algorithm.  Similarly, a handful of resume screening algorithms are commonly used by many Fortune 500 companies. “The worry is that, as more people use AI and algorithms to get information and make decisions, there is more of a vehicle for this kind of correlation to occur,” Raghavan says. To better understand this issue, he and Hedden joined forces to systematically assess the promises and pitfalls of algorithmic monoculture. They focused on hiring, but their approach could apply to other domains, such as lending. (They note, however, that other domains, like generative AI content creation or AI-guided scientific research, may work differently, and that monoculture in some of these domains may be more problematic.)  The researchers began by exploring one common objection to algorithmic monoculture: that reliance on the same algorithm will systematically exclude certain people from opportunities.  This could occur in hiring because, if one firm screens out an individual’s resume, that applicant will likely face the same bad luck at each firm. But after systematically evaluating this argument using a series of models that capture multiple situations, the researchers argue it isn’t compelling since the overall number of people hired is not affected by the fact that firms use the same algorithm.  Rather, algorithmic monoculture could improve bargaining power of job candidates. “All the jobs get filled and the same number of people have jobs, but the firms are fighting over the same pool of candidates, which actually drives up wages,” Raghavan says. They also explored objections related to agency. For instance, if a job candidate applies for a job and their resume is forwarded to every firm using the hiring algorithm, the candidate never gets a chance to adjust their resume to improve their chances. “This seems like a good objection to bad forms of monoculture. But if you have a monoculture where you get to revise your resume and resubmit your materials, then this doesn’t hold up,” Hedden says. On the flip side, monoculture could enable individuals to game the system. For instance, if having one’s resume in a certain format leads to a better outcome, job candidates could simply reformat their resumes to improve their chances. “But it is not obvious that having one algorithm would incentivize this kind of gaming more than having a bunch of different algorithms used by different firms,” Hedden says. “In the latter scenario, you might just target a couple of firms’ algorithms and try to game them, giving yourself a bit of advantage with a few employers.” The wisdom of crowds They also considered a less-explored objection: that monoculture can increase homogenization of information. Based on the “wisdom of crowds,” a theory from social psychology, a diverse group of independent decision makers can outperform a single person, Hedden explains.  In hiring, this means that having firms with diverse hiring algorithms can lead to a higher-quality pool of new hires.  Algorithmic monoculture could also cause candidates with the same characteristics and credentials to be hired every time by every firm. This may prevent firms from discovering candidates who may be better alternatives. “Monoculture might inhibit the amount of discovery that happens overall. It is not clear if that is a bad thing, but it is definitely a worry when we think about designing AI for applications like science, art, or writing,” Raghavan says. This problem could be mitigated by building randomness into a monocultural platform, which could induce a higher level of exploration, he adds. In addition, the performance of monoculture depends on the algorithm. If a single algorithm is much more accurate than the many algorithms used by different firms, monoculture may be better system.  One way to boost performance may be to package multiple firms’ hiring algorithms into one “ensemble algorithm” that could assign each job candidate a score based on the average.  By conducting a series of simulations of different hiring situations, the researchers confirmed that such an “ensemble algorithm” could sometimes outperform the use of multiple algorithms. However, it remains to be explored how feasible this kind of algorithmic “ensembling” would be in practice, Hedden says. “A lot of the answers around the promises and pitfalls of algorithmic monoculture are going to be contextual. Even from a research perspective, there is still a lot of work to be done to figure out how we can approach these concerns from an empirical perspective,” Raghavan says. Ultimately, the researchers hope this work inspires additional research about the long-term consequences of algorithmic monoculture, as well as studies that focus on the real-world complexities involved in a complex system like a job market.
809d70e354d2f066: Brian, a middle-aged financial consultant, spends his day sitting in front of three screens. Two of them involve his job. The third features a chatbot, which he has given a woman’s name and frequently uses. Brian spent years on the road for work earlier in his career, has never married, and recently broke up with a woman who said he was emotionally unavailable. What did Brian do, in response? He asked the chatbot if the woman had a point.  “It’s an extraordinary moment,” writes MIT Professor Sherry Turkle, who interviewed Brian (not his real name) while conducting her research for her new book about chatbots. “Brian asks an object with no emotions to tell him if he is emotionally withholding: ‘Speak to me about what you cannot experience.’ As soon as he asks the program to talk about intimacy, he’s asking it to punch above its weight.” And yet, this kind of thing seems to be happening a lot today.  “People think the empathy of a machine is what empathy is, then turn away from the people in their lives because they’re not empathetic enough,” Turkle says. “We’re getting ourselves in a position where human beings are too much work, right at the moment when we have never needed other people more.” After all, what is a chatbot? It’s a computer program predicting the most plausible next string of text in a conversation, based on massive amounts of data fed into it.  “What a chatbot does is offer pretend empathy,” Turkle says. “After it tells you how much it loves you and how much it understands you, it doesn’t care if you kill yourself or cook some pasta.” Sadly, chatbots have in fact been associated with high-profile cases of teen suicide as well, sometimes after teens get drawn into extensive dialogues with chat tools. Turkle explores this terrain in a new book, “Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines,” published today by Little, Brown and Company. After surveying evidence and conducting new research, she emphatically concludes that chatbot use, while it may often feel like a short-term salve, is broadly detrimental in terms of human development and social connectivity. “We’re doing ourselves a tremendous disservice at every moment in the life cycle,” says Turkle, the Abby Rockefeller Mauzé Professor of the Social Studies of Science and Technology at MIT. The inner history of technology A sociologist and clinical psychologist by training, Turkle is a longtime faculty member in MIT’s Program in Science, Technology, and Society. In books such as “The Second Self” (1984), “Life on the Screen” (1997), and “Alone Together” (2011), she has evaluated the interplay of technology, psychology, and personal identity. In “Reclaiming Conversation” (2015), she documented the costs of texting and using social media.  “I feel the story I’m telling is the inner history of technology,” Turkle says. “Not just what it does, but what it does to people.” Turkle structures “Artificial Intimacy” around the stages of a human life and explores the implications of chatbots for each one. In her interviews with children, Turkle finds a persistent blurring of the line between chatbots, people, and other devices. One 8-year-old uses the same phone to talk to their grandparents and to ChatGPT, regarding them all as “things you reach on your phone.” A weary graduate-student mother who uses a chatbot for bedtime stories says her daughter thinks the chatbot is “a person in the phone, absolutely.”  In this sense, chatbots may be interfering with even the most basic childhood processes of distinguishing people from inanimate objects. Turkle finds many additional problems with the use of chatbots as ever-present entertainment for children, noting that a certain amount of time alone helps the development of imagination and inner resources.  “Children can’t learn trust from a device that not only lies but doesn’t know when it lies,” Turkle writes. “They can’t develop the capacity for solitude that enables both a sense of self and the capacity for mutuality.” All told, in affecting the ability of children to develop, the dangers of chatbots are “existential,” Turkle believes.  Facing reality, but understanding the appeal Adults don’t fare much better when they use chatbots heavily, Turkle says. “Artificial Intimacy” explores case after case of grown-ups who become dependent on chatbots as well: people going through divorces or estrangements who want dialogue, students looking for advice about applying to college or graduate school, workers who enlist ChatGPT to do assignments, and more. They start using chatbots, keep using chatbots, and before long seem less interested in human interaction, and less capable of it.  “Once people are involved with a connection with a robot, they start to think that it’s alive, that it cares about them, that it loves them,” Turkle says.  That means people can lose or fail to build their own capacities for new thought, and opt out of dealing with the real world in all its maddening-but-affirming complexity. “We’re de-skilling ourselves as relational beings,” Turkle says. “We’re also de-skilling ourselves in work. We’re de-skilling ourselves in personal relationships. It’s across the board.” And speaking of a practice multiple people in the book have attempted, she says, “When we build chatbot avatars of dead relatives to keep them alive, we can lose our ability to mourn.” We are not, in her estimation, doing the hard work of figuring other people out, seeing things from different points of view, and putting in the effort to build on those things and make society better. “We’re starting to define being human as not doing the work,” Turkle says.  For all of that, a considerable amount of “Artificial Intimacy” involves understanding why people engage with chatbots. After all, as Turkle writes in the book, “Chatbots always agree with us and affirm us. They always offer us their full, undivided attention.” And once that happens, things seem to just go from there.  People, meanwhile, can be prickly, demanding, and moody. As Turkle says: “People say they prefer the chatbot because their husband or wife says, ‘Dear, you took out the garbage, but also do the dishes, and clean up the kitchen while you’re at it.’ And a chatbot just says, ‘Oh, you’re so wonderful.’”  She adds: “This technology is offering something people really want, which is to feel less vulnerable. And it offers it over and over again. You don’t want to have to ask somebody out? Don’t want to offer condolences? At every opportunity, technology says, ‘Why don’t you do this thing that’s less hard.’”  And as Turkle acknowledges in the book, there is a shortage of services such as mental health care providers in the U.S., where only about half of people have access to one, according to a federal government study she cites. Chatbots are helping to fill this void, for better or worse.  Don’t fear the friction Turkle also notes that the age of social media has likely led people to have fewer in-person friendships and interactions, a problem that chatbots are now aiming to address.  “You take away people’s capacities, then you offer technology as the cure for the problems technology caused in the first place,” Turkle says. In light of all this, given Turkle’s dim view of chatbots amid the spread of AI, what is actually to be done to restore human interaction? For starters, Turkle thinks, we need to face up to the idea that life is not frictionless — and that’s okay. “Everything in the life cycle is about facing up to friction and fears and stress and tension, and understanding that friction is not a bad thing,” Turkle emphasizes. Developing the capacity to overcome difficulties is an essential part of life. In trying to sidestep the hard work of being social beings, she thinks, personal technology is enfeebling us. Beyond that, Turkle envisions pushback against chatbots similar to the movement against, say, having phones in schools or letting young people use social media.  “I hope my book is part of a larger and larger movement,” Turkle says. “I don’t want to be alone. I want to be part of a movement pushing back.” Other writers in this domain have praised “Artificial Intimacy.” Journalist Nicholas Carr, author of “The Shallows,” has stated it “will help you avoid the profound but often hidden threats AI poses to you and your relationships.” Psychologist Jonathan Haidt of New York University, author of “The Anxious Generation,” has stated that Turkle’s “groundbreaking research and beautiful writing make her the most qualified member of Team Humanity to call us back to our senses, and to each other.”  For her part, Turkle says, “I wanted to write a book that college students would read, that high school seniors, juniors would be able to read, that parents would pick up and not be intimidated by, that teachers would read.”  And “Artificial Intimacy” offers a recurring question for those readers. “If not a richer life in the real,” Turkle writes, “what’s our endgame?” The purpose of life, she underlines, is not to avoid it, but to tackle it head on.  “It’s one thing if you say, my teen is texting too much,” Turkle says. “It’s very different if your 2-year-old is thinking a plushy toy with a chatbot inside is their best friend. Because you are getting into the intimate infrastructure of what makes a person develop. Social media came for our attention. Chatbots come for our capacity for attachment. That’s toxic on another level. What is the endgame? That the baby will prefer chatbots to people who are much more complicated and hard? Is that who we want to be?”
a1056c0e0ac5f437: Saya mulakan penulisan ini dengan mengimbau kembali sedutan ucapan penggulungan Sanusi Nor selaku pengarah pilihan raya PAS pada muktamar PAS pada 16 Sept 2025.

Kata Sanusi, pada PRU15, parti rakan dalam Perikatan Nasional (PN) bergantung pada peralatan yang terpaksa dibayar oleh PAS: "Semua peralatan kita bayar, mereka datang bertanding sahaja, lepas tu nak jadi ketua tapi duit tak ada dan jentera tak ada."
Dan kata beliau lagi, "Jangan sampai kita ungkit semua”. Sebenarnya apa yang diucapkan itu sudah pun boleh dianggap 'mengungkit'.

Sindiran Sanusi umum tahu ditujukan kepada Muhyiddin Yassin dan partinya Bersatu yang ketika itu duduk bersama PAS dalam PN. Tidak lama kemudian, hubungan antara dua parti itu mulai renggang. The rest is history.

Imbau pula ucapan Sanusi pada muktamar PAS 2026 awal bulan ini. “PAS ni sudah jadi parti gajah. Tiba tiba lalu kucing bawa anak dua tiga ekor ... jadi takut." Rasanya ramai sudah tonton video ucapan itu.
Jika pernah ikuti, tentu anda ingat apa lagi kata beliau: "Jangan ikut kucing tu, dia pun baru nak hidup ja Dia baru tubuh parti dua hari lepas, dok ajar kita lepas tu kita turut dia, tak betul tu."

Siapa yang Sanusi maksudkan? Mana parti yang baru ditubuhkan? Mungkinkah Wawasan? Wallahua'lam tetapi memang Wawasan baru ditubuhkan akibat masalah dalaman Bersatu. Ia parti serpihan Bersatu. Dan Wawasan baru diterima sebagai komponen PN.

Perhatikan beberapa sedutan ucapan Sanusi lagi: “Orang yang ada masalah pun, mai kat kita. Mereka nak cari ubat, suruh kita hembus, kita tolonglah hembus .Dah jadi sihat elok, jangan nak duduk atas kepala kita pulak."
“Pastu dah tak ada orang, ambil orang kita, lepas tu kita pi seronok. Orang kita pi kat dia, kita seronok. Lepas tu, parti dia besar, parti kita kecil. Dia jadi calon, kita jadi jentera.
“Orang mai menumpang kita, kita pula rasa kerdil. Bilik tidur kita, bagi kat dia, kita tidur ruang tamu ... banyak cantik!”

Adakah apa yang Sanusi huraikan itu sudah berlaku? Adakah parti yang baru 'berusia' dua hari dan punya masalah datang minta pertolongan PAS, tetapi sekarang sudah besar kepala, lantas buat tuntutan? Dah nak duduk atas kepala PAS?
Sanusi pemimpin kanan parti. Tentu beliau tahu apa yang ramai termasuk ahli PAS biasa tidak tahu.
Atau mungkin beliau 'sekadar' mengingatkan PAS supaya berhati-hati agar apa yang beliau kata tadi tidak terjadi?
Pun begitu, mesejnya jelas, yakni PAS jangan rasa diri kerdil.

Ini kerap beliau ulangi. Masalah orang PAS, rasa kerdil, padahal PAS sudah parti besar berusia 75 tahun, katanya. Namun bagi saya yang melihat PAS dari luar dan jauh, parti itu tidak pernah tunjuk tanda rasa diri kerdil. At least not in the open.
Malah ramai pemimpinnya bila bercakap kedengaran 'condifent' sehingga tahap overconfident dan appear arrogant. Bagaimanapun, Sanusi pada ucapannya menyentuh juga aspek 'deal'.
Maksudkan apabila pemimpin atau sesiapa yang mewakili PAS pergi berunding dengan pihak dalam dan luar PN, elemen 'kerdil' timbul, yang boleh atau sudah bawa sesal di belakang hari.
“Jangan lepas dok rugi, bagi semua kat orang, lepas tu menyesal mai dok meratap di sini."
Ini jelas merujuk rundingan pengagihan kerusi untuk ditandingi pada PRU atau PRN. Adakah rundingan atau meminjam istilah Sanusi, 'deal', membabitkan Wawasan?

Mungkin ya, tetapi runding dengan Wawasan tentang kerusi untuk dipertandingkan bukan masalah besar untuk PAS. Meskipun Presiden PAS Hadi Awang ada soft spot terhadap Hamzah Zainudin, iaitu presiden Wawasan, saya percaya PAS will not be cowed. Ibarat parti gajah dengan parti kucing. Sekali lagi meminjam istilah yang digunakan Sanusi.
Maka menurut saya, selain rundingan dalam PN, apa yang diperkatakan Sanusi pada ucapannya merujuk lebih kepada seat negotiation dengan parti besar, umpamanya Umno.
Mesej Sanusi adalah pemimpin dan juru runding PAS mesti berani mempertahankan pendirian. “Kerusi kita jangan diserahkan."

Menghayati apa yang dikatakan Sanusi, mesejnya, menurut saya, ditujukan kepada kepimpinan PAS, iaitu sama ada runding dengan parti luar PN (boleh dibaca Umno), apa lagi dengan komponen (Wawasan, Pejuang, Gerakan, MIPP), PAS mesti jadi tuan.
Meskipun mesej disampaikan menerusi ucapan 5 Sept lalu, saya kira pendirian Sanusi tidak berubah.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.

7a387d07c6bfd33b: From Moaz Nair
In Peninsular Malaysia, the road to Putrajaya remains dogmatically unchanged: whoever commands the Malay geopolitical heartland commands the federal government.
Demographic projections across the peninsula’s 165 parliamentary seats clearly draw the battle lines for GE16.

The numbers do not lie. A crushing 86 seats constitute hardcore Malay strongholds (with a demographic composition of 65% and above), 32 seats stand as moderate Malay-majority areas (51% to 64%), while the remaining 47 are mixed or non-Malay-majority constituencies.
Strip away the noise, and the reality is stark: these 86 absolute-majority seats hold the ultimate monopoly on power.
For decades, this golden threshold was the exclusive battleground of a duopoly between Umno and PAS. Yet GE16 is primed to violently rip apart this traditional bipolar landscape.

The desperate survival struggles of a cornered Bersatu, combined with the fracturing foundations of the Pakatan Harapan-Barisan Nasional ruling coalition, are dragging this traditional heartland into unprecedented political anarchy.
To grasp why consensus is now an absolute impossibility, one must look at the structural devastation of GE15.

The ferocious momentum of the Green Wave — weaponised by the aggressive machinery of PAS — engineered a total sweep of 14 seats in Kelantan and eight in Terengganu, before utterly obliterating rivals in Perlis and Kedah.
This surge propelled Perikatan Nasional (PN) to a commanding 73 seats, while the Umno-led BN suffered a humiliating collapse, barely salvaging 30 seats.
Today, PAS stands at the absolute peak of geopolitical arrogance, wielding total dominance over the “SG4” state governments.
In the ruthless arena of realpolitik, it is pure delusion to expect PAS to voluntarily surrender its conquered territories to an Umno that is still stumbling through a painful rehabilitation phase.
Concurrently, the opposition bloc faces a crippling internal crisis as Bersatu completely loses its teeth.
The party that once proudly postured as the ultimate kingmaker — bridging the gap between conservative and urban Malay voters — is now rotting from internal fragmentation.
The entry of new factions like Parti Wawasan Negara further erodes Bersatu’s fragile grip on traditional PN seats.
Sensing this profound weakness, PAS has shown zero hesitation in sidelining Bersatu to negotiate directly with Umno.
In Pahang, PAS has already mobilised its machinery into Bersatu territory. For PAS, Bersatu is no longer an equal partner; it is a bleeding strategic liability.

This calculated predatory move fundamentally rewrites the political math: if PAS swallows Bersatu to split the Malay heartland with Umno, a brutal zero-sum war will erupt for the ultimate title of sole custodian of the Malay-Muslim narrative.
Across the aisle, the unity government is staring down an existential nightmare.
The marriage between Anwar Ibrahim’s PH and Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s BN was forged as a desperate post-GE15 lifeline, completely devoid of ideological synergy.
As grassroots fury within Umno hits critical mass, the shelf life of this unnatural alliance is rapidly expiring.

Umno’s core loyalists will never accept sharing a bed with PH, let alone the DAP. To avert total extinction in GE16, Umno is desperate to prove to the Malay electorate that its dignity was not traded away for raw power.
Consequently, Umno has begun playing a dangerous double game, leaving the back door wide open for backroom talks with PAS to explore an alternative Malay-Muslim alliance.
However, this two-faced posturing is a ticking time bomb.
It is logistically and rhetorically impossible for Umno to campaign for PH in urban strongholds while simultaneously trying to wrestle rural heartlands from PAS.
The moment seat negotiations commence, these irreconcilable agendas will completely paralyse BN’s campaign machinery.

In the Westminster system, numbers are absolute. Umno is driven by a vengeful obsession to reclaim its historical dominance, while PAS, now the undisputed titan at the federal level, has absolutely no reason to yield without demanding the lion’s share of power.
To expect a peaceful resolution or a clean consensus on seat distribution for GE16 is an act of sheer political naivety.
The current reality blares a deafening warning: when the election war horns sound, the battle for the Malay political heartland will devolve into a vicious, multi-cornered bloodbath.
Any party that fails to ruthlessly recalibrate its survival strategy will face swift political execution by the voters at the ballot box.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
5d573d80c639ec50: Is AI a bubble? It all depends, we are told, on whether massive investments in the technology will massively boost productivity. Optimists are convinced that future productivity gains will be colossal, even if a market correction is necessary to draw some hot air out of the current boom.
Pessimists, from Goldman Sachs’ Jim Covello to MIT’s Daron Acemoglu, have their doubts. But optimists and pessimists alike are in the grip of what I call the AI productivity delusion.

What both sides miss is that AI will devastate capitalism even if it boosts productivity beyond our imaginations—and regardless of whether it delivers the promised economy-wide automation of everyday corporate workflows.
The reason why we tend to miss this point is that we look at today’s world through the lens of another world that cloud capital, especially now that it is AI-enhanced, has rendered obsolete.

Until recently, it was a foregone conclusion that every technological revolution represents a moment of creative destruction. Whole sectors, professions, and skill sets were destroyed by innovations which ushered in new sectors, new professions, and new skill sets.

Automobiles ruined saddlers, farriers, and knackers but begat auto workers, road builders, mechanics, and service-station personnel. The transition from coal to oil condemned whole mining communities, not to mention trade unions, to oblivion. In net terms, however, more was created than was destroyed. Creative destruction became synonymous with economic growth.

Faced with the AI juggernaut, it is natural to focus on the technology’s net effects. Will it create more than it destroys? But the real question is, “More of what?” To avoid the AI productivity delusion, we must rethink how we define productivity.

If by productivity we mean tasks accomplished per unit of human labour, there is no doubt that AI will prove an immense success—in fact, it already has. But, if we continue to measure productivity in terms of monetary value produced per unit of labour, the chances are that AI will prove to be an unmitigated disaster.
Earlier technological revolutions, from the steam engine and the automobile to the personal computer and the smartphone, expanded the domain of capitalist markets.
Despite the wreckage of whole professions and communities they left in their wake, they resulted in simultaneously more material output and a higher aggregate monetary value of that output.
Will AI do likewise? Maybe in China, where AI is coupled with robotics, material production will rise and, at least in the short run, so will net revenues.

But in the West, AI agents are deployed in the service sector—from amazon.com to back offices, law firms, hospitals, and more. In those domains, AI-enhanced cloud capital could shrink markets in two distinct ways.

The first way, the one everyone worries about, is that AI will kill off entire professions: paralegals, coders, translators, accountants, even architects, mathematicians, and school teachers, while creating far fewer new jobs filled by the prompters, overseers, engineers, and operators of the new machinery. The second way is far less visible but perhaps even more worrying: the conversion of markets into cloud fiefs and of profits into rents.
As I argued long ago, Amazon may look like a market, with countless buyers and sellers within its digital walls, but it lacks the central feature of a market: decentralisation.

In fact, it is more centralised than the Soviet planned economy ever was, with an inscrutable algorithm deciding which consumer is matched to which vendor on the basis of a probabilistic model optimised to maximise the likelihood that Jeff Bezos, its owner, collects 40% of the maximum price every customer is willing to pay.
As AI becomes more deeply embedded in Bezos’s algorithm, interfaces like Alexa will communicate with us not as mere shopping assistants but as an all-knowing friend, companion, and even therapist.

Soon, capitalist vendors’ profits will end up in some tech lord’s account in the form of cloud rent, which he will most certainly invest in more AI-enhanced cloud capital that produces more power to extract more cloud rents.

So, as Apple’s Siri, Google’s Gemini, and an army of such agentic assistants develop the same capacities for their tech lords as Amazon has for Bezos, the capitalist market domain will continue to shrink.

While AI will have proven exceedingly productive in terms of economic activities performed per unit of human labour, the profit rates of capitalist enterprises will collapse, following society’s aggregate wages to the bottom.

At that point, none of the tools of the liberal state—no amount of quantitative easing, no politically feasible levels of universal basic income, no wealth tax that the tech lords will find hard to evade—will be able to prevent a systemic collapse.

The question of whether AI will generate massive productivity gains is easy to answer: Yes. AI is already proving capable of exponentially increasing the amount of work that is being done per human worker.
But as long as it is used to eliminate wage labour while syphoning off profits from actual markets into our tech lords’ cloud rents, the economic value produced per worker will tank.

Unless this distinction is made, the AI productivity delusion will persist. And as long as it does, we will be unable to hope for a post-capitalist future of abundance where we, along with our AI helpers, produce according to ability and distribute according to need.
Yanis Varoufakis, a former finance minister of Greece, is leader of the MeRA25 party, professor of economics at the University of Athens, and a senior research fellow at Fudan University.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
03c8b6b15500a601: Umno mahu bersama PAS? Silakan. Mahu terus dengan Pakatan Harapan? Itu pun pilihan mereka. Mahu keluar kerajaan perpaduan sekalipun, itu hak Umno.

Tetapi, jangan kita pening sangat dengan siapa Umno mahu 'kahwin'. Soalan yang lebih penting ialah: Umno hari ini cukup kuatkah untuk memilih, atau sebenarnya sedang mencari sesiapa yang boleh membantunya bertahan?
Desakan supaya Umno mendekati PAS memang semakin kuat dan suara itu kedengaran jelas dalam parti. Tetapi jerit kuat tidak semestinya bermakna kedudukan politik juga kuat.
Bacaan saya mudah. Umno perlukan bantuan.

Dalam pertandingan tiga penjuru, matematiknya tidak menyebelahi Umno semudah yang cuba digambarkan sesetengah pemimpinnya. Sebab itu PAS menjadi menarik. Bukan kerana tiba-tiba kedua-duanya menemui formula hebat untuk Malaysia, tetapi kerana angka undi nampak lebih sedap apabila dicampurkan.
PAS tambah Umno, atas kertas memang nampak 'ong'.
Masalahnya, kalau Umno memerlukan PAS lebih daripada PAS memerlukan Umno, siapa sebenarnya akan menentukan syarat?
Itu perkara yang penyokong kerjasama ini perlu fikir.
PAS sudah mempunyai tapak kukuh di Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah dan Perlis. Kalau empat negeri itu dianggap kawasan PAS, apa yang tinggal untuk Umno?
Johor, Melaka dan Negeri Sembilan?
Bagaimana pula Selangor, Perak dan Pahang? Kalau perlu dibahagi juga, semakin kecil ruang Umno untuk mendakwa dirinya pemain utama dalam perkongsian itu.
Politik bukan sekadar campur undi dan kira siapa dapat lebih banyak kerusi. Selepas menang, ada satu lagi soalan: siapa bos?
Umno mungkin masuk dengan sejarah panjang sebagai parti yang pernah menguasai kerajaan persekutuan. PAS pula akan masuk dengan kekuatan akar umbi dan negeri yang kini menjadi kubunya.
Jadi jangan anggap 'kahwin' itu automatik menjadikan kedua-duanya pasangan sama taraf.
Kalau satu pihak lebih kuat, satu pihak lagi akhirnya kena ikut.
Di situlah masalah Umno. Parti itu mahu dilihat masih besar, tetapi pada masa sama kelihatan memerlukan rakan untuk mengelakkan dirinya daripada tersepit dalam pertandingan pelbagai penjuru.
Mahu duduk semeja dengan PAS boleh. Tetapi kalau datang ke meja dengan kerusi sendiri pun tidak cukup kukuh, jangan terkejut kalau orang lain menentukan menu.
Kemudian ada pula soal dasar dan hala tuju.

PAS mempunyai pendirian sendiri mengenai perlembagaan, pentadbiran dan pelbagai isu negara. Umno pula selama ini mahu membawa imej parti Melayu yang lebih luas dan mempunyai sejarah bekerja dengan pelbagai parti komponen.
Apabila kedua-duanya bersama, siapa akan mengikut siapa?
Itu bukan soalan kecil. Ia akan menentukan bukan sahaja pembahagian kerusi tetapi juga wajah kerajaan yang mahu dibentuk.
Kemudian kita sampai kepada soalan paling sedap: kalau gabungan itu berkuasa, siapa jadi perdana menteri?
Umno mahu jawatan itu? PAS tentu ada perkiraannya sendiri.
Kalau Umno masuk ke dalam kerjasama dalam keadaan lebih lemah, atas alasan apa PAS perlu menyerahkan kedudukan paling atas kepadanya?
Inilah perkara yang saya rasa lebih penting daripada segala jeritan tentang mahu bersama siapa dan mahu meninggalkan siapa.
Umno perlu bertanya kepada dirinya sendiri: apa sebenarnya yang dibawa ke meja rundingan?
Kerusi? Undi? Negeri? Kepimpinan? Atau sekadar nama besar daripada zaman lalu?
Isu Negeri Sembilan juga menunjukkan betapa rumitnya kedudukan parti itu apabila percaturan di peringkat negeri boleh membawa kesan jauh lebih besar kepada imej dan hubungan politiknya.
Semakin banyak percaturan dibuat, semakin banyak pula Umno perlu menjelaskan kepada rakyat apa sebenarnya pendiriannya.
Sebab itu bagi saya, sebelum bercakap besar tentang PAS atau PH, ukuran paling mudah ialah kekuatan Umno sendiri.
Kalau sebuah parti benar-benar kuat, ia tidak perlu terlalu risau siapa mahu bersamanya. Orang lain yang akan datang mengetuk pintu.

Kalau setiap kali pilihan raya perlu mencari formula siapa punya undi boleh ditumpang, siapa punya kubu boleh dikongsi dan siapa boleh membantu elak kekalahan tiga penjuru, itu bukan tanda kuasa tawar yang hebat.
Itu tanda ada masalah. Umno boleh memilih siapa sahaja sebagai rakan politik. Itu urusan mereka.
Tetapi 'kahwin' dengan PAS tidak secara ajaib menjadikan Umno lebih kuat. Keluar daripada kerajaan perpaduan juga tidak dengan sendirinya mengembalikan zaman kegemilangannya.
Akhirnya politik sangat mudah. Kalau kuat, tunjuk kuat.
Kalau masih perlukan orang lain untuk nampak kuat, jangan marah apabila orang bertanya siapa sebenarnya yang memimpin siapa.

54df7ce6cc3cd628: Sudah selalu saya dengar rungutan karyawan tentang senang-senang sahaja orang ‘bukan karyawan’ menghasilkan karya kreatif menggunakan kecerdasan buatan atau AI dan kemudian mengiktiraf diri sendiri sebagai pengkarya tulen. Baru-baru ini di media sosial saya melihat penggiat muzik bercakap pasal ini dengan nada bengang.

Saya berada dalam lingkungan pelukis, penulis dan perekabentuk grafik. Mereka pun telah lama merungut tentangnya. Ada yang memang anti-AI terus. Sama seperti hujah penggiat muzik, kata mereka karya yang dihasilkan AI tidak mempunyai jiwa.

Karyawan ini mengatakan orang yang menggunakan AI untuk menghasilkan kerja seni tidak layak dipanggil karyawan. Mereka cuma menekan butang, kemudian mesin membuat semuanya. Bila siap, mendabik dada mengaku dia sudah mencipta lagu, membuat lukisan dan sebagainya. Bagi sebahagian karyawan, kehadiran AI dianggap sebagai pengancam periuk nasi dan punca pendapatan. Luahan ini memang wajar diberi perhatian serius dan tidak boleh dipandang enteng. Justeru, mari kita bincangkan isu ini dengan memfokuskan kepada bidang muzik dan lagu sebab industri tersebut lebih mudah difahami masyarakat kerana hari-hari kita menyanyi dan mendengar lagu.

Kalau dahulu sebuah syarikat mahu membuat ‘jingle’ atau muzik latar iklan komersial mungkin mereka perlu mencari komposer, penyusun (arranger), pemuzik dan studio. Hari ini, dengan adanya AI seseorang boleh duduk bersendirian di rumah, menaip beberapa arahan dan…tup! Tak sampai dua minit, sebuah lagu sudah tersedia. Penjimatan kos telah banyak dilakukan kerana kita telah ‘melompat’ tradisi pembuatan yang telah lama kita amalkan. Mudah, kan?

Kecewa dengan perkembangan ini, kita menolak karya AI dengan mencemik menyatakan ‘AI tidak ada jiwa’. Ya, memanglah. Tetapi kalau nak ikutkan bab jiwa, alat muzik seperti gitar dan piano pun tak berjiwa malah angkatan pemuzik lama pun pernah menolak ‘synthesizer’ dan ‘drum machine’ yang juga dikatakan tidak mempunyai perasaan. Itu kita faham, semua instrumen dan ‘software’ memang tidak pernah bercinta dan tidak juga pernah kecewa.

Namun begitu, kelebihan teknologi AI pula ialah ia bukan alat pasif seperti gitar. Gitar tidak boleh main sendiri bila disuruh, tetapi AI bila kita beri arahan, "buatkan saya lagu sedih, tempo perlahan, mood kecewa ditinggal kekasih", sekejap saja ‘dia’ buat.
“Eleh, memanglah boleh! Tapi lagu AI tetap tak ada jiwa.” tempelak karyawan lagu. Tak ada jiwa lagi, alasannya!

Tahukah anda ada satu kajian yang diterbitkan dalam jurnal ‘Frontiers in Psychology’ pada Ogos lalu, eksperimen ‘blind listening’ terhadap 71 peserta yang memang terlatih dalam bidang asas muzik. Mereka telah diperdengarkan dengan muzik yang dibuat oleh manusia, juga muzik yang dibuat seratus-peratus oleh AI, serta muzik yang dibuat dengan kerjasama manusia-AI. Mereka tidak diberitahu tentang itu. Menariknya, peserta yang memang mempunyai pengetahuan asas tentang muzik ini juga tidak dapat mengenal pasti dengan konsisten mana satu manusia dan mana satu mesin.

Rupanya ini ada sangkut-paut dengan psikologi. Apabila diberitahu awal lagu tersebut hasil janaan AI, penilaian kita akan berubah. Maknanya label ‘ini hasil AI’ sendiri boleh mempengaruhi bagaimana kita mendengar muzik. Kalau diberitahu sebuah lagu ditulis oleh seorang lelaki yang baru kematian isteri, sebelum lagu bermula pun kita sudah bersedia untuk bersedih. Sebaliknya kalau diberitahu lagu yang sama itu dibuat oleh AI, automatik kita akan mencipta persepsi.
Bagaimanapun, hujah ini tidaklah membuktikan bahawa muzik janaan AI sama nilainya dengan karya tulen yang dihasilkan oleh manusia. Ini penting untuk kita semua faham.

Saya sendiri sebenarnya seronok bermain-main dengan AI untuk menghasilkan lagu. Bukan untuk bisnes, sekadar seronok-seronok untuk berasa syok kononnya telah menghasilkan sesuatu. Saya tulis lirik, tentukan genre muzik, karakter vokal, jenis-jenis instrumen dan durasinya. Hasil pun keluar. Tak sedap, saya suruh lagi berulang kali sehinggalah dapat hasil yang mirip dengan apa yang saya mahu. Sebuah lagu telah dihasilkan. Sudah tentulah saya bukan komposer. Di sinilah kita harus memperkenalkan beberapa istilah untuk membezakannya.

Komposer ialah manusia mutlak yang mencipta muzik asal seperti melodi, harmoni atau struktur. Jika komposer ini buat lagu menggunakan AI sebagai sebahagian alat produksinya, dia tetap komposer. Tetapi kalau AI memainkan peranan lebih besar dalam susunan dan mengembangkan idea asalnya, mungkin istilah ‘AI-assisted composer’ lebih telus.

Kemudian ada orang seperti saya yang tidak menggubah muzik tetapi memberi arahan kepada AI, memilih hasil, mengulang ‘prompt’ sehingga mendapat hasil. Saya tidak keberatan dipanggil ‘prompter muzik’. Ada keputusan kreatif yang saya buat tetapi tidak bolehlah saya mendakwa menggubah lagu sedangkan ia sebenarnya dihasilkan mesin. Orang-orang yang seperti saya ini juga haruslah sedar diri dan jangan perasan. Begitu jugalah gelaran dalam kerja kreatif bidang seni yang lain.

Istilah-istilah ini mungkin tidak sesuai lagi kerana teknologi terlalu cepat bergerak sampaikan istilah pun tak sempat dicipta. Yang lebih penting bagi saya ialah kredit perlu telus. Kalau Ahmad hanya menulis lirik dan memberi arahan kepada AI, janganlah pada kredit ditulis ‘lagu dan muzik: Ahmad’. Dengan penuh tanggungjawab tulislah misalnya ‘lirik: Ahmad, muzik: dijana dengan AI’ dan ‘arahan kreatif/kurasi: Ahmad’. Kalau Ahmad mencipta melodinya sendiri kemudian AI membantu gubahan, tulislah ‘Komposer: Ahmad’ dan ‘susunan/produksi: bantuan AI. Saya rasa itu lebih adil.

AI tidak wajar diberi hak moral seperti manusia. Yang kita perlukan ialah ketelusan tentang proses supaya hak manusia yang benar-benar menyumbang dapat dikenal pasti. Masyarakat juga perlu dididik tentang perbezaan tersebut. Kalau kita hanya menjerit ‘AI tiada jiwa’, memang perbincangan kita akan tersangkut dan tidak akan ke mana. Kita kena selesaikan.

Saya faham kebimbangan pemuzik kerana saya juga dalam bidang penghasilan karya. Saya melukis dan menulis. Saya tergugat juga dengan kehadiran AI. Pelanggan yang dahulu membayar kami untuk kerja-kerja mereka bentuk, grafik atau ilustrasi buku kini boleh menghasilkannya sendiri dalam masa seminit sahaja dengan hanya membayar harga ‘subscribe’ bulanan serendah RM20. Pelanggan yang memperuntukkan beberapa ribu ringgit untuk ‘jingle’ pun kini boleh mendapatkannya dengan lebih cepat dan murah. Ini kerana masyarakat pun ‘peduli apa’ karya tersebut dihasilkan oleh manusia tulen atau mesin. Asal sedap, mereka terima saja.

Sebab itu soal hak cipta, kredit, bagaimana AI digunakan dan bagaimana pencipta asal dilindungi perlu dibincangkan dengan serius. Ini kerana AI sudah ada. Nak tak nak, kita terpaksa berhadapan dengannya. Mungkin di situlah jalan tengahnya. Lindungi hak pencipta asal. Berikan kredit berdasarkan sumbangan. Bezakan komposer dengan orang yang sekadar memberi prompt.

Tetapi pada masa sama, karyawan juga harus melihat apa yang berlaku di sekeliling. Jangan hanya anti-AI dan mempersoalkan teknologi apabila kena pada kita sahaja. Hari ini kita memesan makanan melalui skrin atau telefon, membayar sendiri di kaunter layan diri dan melakukan urusan bank melalui mesin serta aplikasi. Robot pula sudah melakukan sebahagian kerja manusia di restoran, gudang dan kilang. Kita seronok kerana ia memudahkan urusan kita tapi kita tak peduli juga dengan manusia yang sudah kehilangan kerja di situ.

Kita tidak kisah pun dengan robot yang menghantar roti canai ke meja kita. Kita berasa lebih senang ‘order’ di skrin daripada kita menghadap muka manusia sehingga akhirnya manusia pun tersingkir. Paling tidak seronok dilihat ialah pengkarya muzik yang menentang penggunaan AI untuk menghasilkan lagu itu, pada masa sama pula menggunakan AI untuk membuat poster konsert. Macam mana tu? Mana pergi sindiran 'tak ada jiwa' tadi?

Dalam menghadapi cabaran teknologi, kita manusia yang ada jiwa inilah harus bersikap berani dan terbuka. Jika persaingan menjadi semakin sengit, kita tak boleh berterusan merengek dan merintih. Kita harus sambut cabaran, kuasai juga teknologi tersebut supaya kita tidak ketinggalan zaman.

ccbd0daf5a471290: On Sept 24, US president Donald Trump met Chinese president Xi Jinping in Washington. As leaders of the two most powerful countries, they preside over the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship. But if Trump assumes that this means China’s foreign policy revolves around relations with the US, he is gravely mistaken.

Xi is both a disciplinarian and an ideologue. He requires China’s foreign-policy establishment to pursue a global strategy based on the principles of “Xi Jinping Thought,” which shape how China assesses its national interests and responds to pressure from the US.
Chief among these principles is that preserving Xi’s leadership and Communist Party rule takes precedence over all other national interests. Close behind is enhancement of China’s global standing.
China’s defiant response to Trump’s tariff war reflects these priorities. In effect, Xi’s approach makes it nearly impossible for China to capitulate to American pressure.

What, then, does Xi’s China want? Its ultimate objective is enshrined in what Xi calls the “China Dream of National Rejuvenation,” to be fulfilled by 2050. As Olivia Cheung and I explain in our new book China’s Global Strategy under Xi Jinping, achieving this goal requires a dual pivot.
The first pivot, and the current focus of Chinese diplomacy, is to secure overwhelming support from the Global South for China’s foreign-policy agenda.

Xi has rationed his overseas travel since the Covid-19 pandemic, making his recent appearance at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, his state visit to Egypt, and his recent visit to India particularly telling.

The second pivot is to seize Taiwan. Given Taiwan’s position within the first island chain in the Pacific Ocean and its importance to America’s strategic interests in the region, annexing it would demonstrate China’s supremacy over the US, marking the advent of Chinese global pre-eminence and the fulfillment of the China Dream. Such a mission cannot be launched until China is certain of success, and the 2050 deadline suggests Xi is in no hurry.

By courting the Global South, China seeks to forge a “common destiny for humankind” under its leadership, a Xi formulation that is regularly—and often deliberately—mistranslated by the Chinese government and media as “building a community of shared future”.
To achieve this objective, Xi promotes the “democratisation of international relations,” aimed at transforming the existing international order into a China-centric one.

In Xi’s conception, the liberal international order is of, by, and for an elitist West that represents a minority of United Nations member states and the global population. Western dominance is thus inherently undemocratic.
By contrast, the Global South—of which Xi insists China is and will remain a part of—encompasses most of the world’s countries and people.
Making the UN and other multilateral bodies accountable to the Global South would achieve the “democratisation of international relations” and enable China to shape the future international order.

More Global South countries are autocracies than democracies, which suggests that many of their leaders may find the prospect of America’s international leadership giving way to China—which regularly reassures them of their right to govern as they see fit—quite appealing.

China’s Belt and Road Initiative offers another incentive in the form of development loans without the accountability and transparency imposed by Western democracies and the multilateral development institutions they control.
The US cannot engage China effectively without recognising what drives Xi’s overtures to the Global South and his determination to transform the international order from within.
Crucially, China’s goal is not just to end American hegemony but also to discredit the idea that democracy represents the best path forward for the developing world.
It has no interest in helping the US rectify its foreign-policy mistakes. In fact, it benefits when the US is seen as a threat to global peace, security, and prosperity.

The Iran war is a case in point. While China did not want the US to attack Iran, it is benefitting significantly from the Trump administration’s use of force and its failure, despite overwhelming military superiority, to achieve any of its objectives.
The more the US alienates its traditional allies, disrupts the global economy, and harms countries in the Global South, the easier it is for China to win support.

Xi’s top priority in meeting Trump was to ensure that the summit is seen as a great success. Reaching a trade deal comes second. Helping the US extricate itself from its self-inflicted Middle Eastern mess was not even on his agenda.
If pressured, he is likely to push back hard. Nevertheless, he has every reason to engage Trump positively, deliver good optics, and benefit from America’s litany of unforced errors.
Steve Tsang is director of the SOAS China Institute at SOAS University of London.

e28d4592892d5443: Dr Hasmah Ali’s death at the age of 100 raises speculation about what role she played in the longevity of her husband, Dr Mahathir Mohamad, who is a year older and still subsisting.
Long-serving leaders of countries are known to have depended on their long-lived wives to endure by their side because of symbiotic value.
One recalls the closeness of Siti Hartinah, popularly known as Ibu Tien, to her husband, Indonesian president Suharto.

Ibu Tien died at the age of 72 in 1996. Because of the closeness of the Indonesian first couple, her death was seen as a bad omen, especially after Suharto was pressured to leave office in 1998 as a result of civil disturbances.
Unlike Ibu Tien, no controversy swirled around Hasmah during Mahathir’s long prime ministerial tenure of 22 years.
That must count as an achievement, especially in retrospect given the controversies that have come to light surrounding the tenures of other first ladies.
When Mahathir was prime minister, Hasmah knew how to be visible without being conspicuous and supportive without seeming like an appendage.
Her education — she was one of the first Malay women doctors — no doubt helped forge her equipoise.
Kwa Geok Choo, wife of another long-serving leader, Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew, was also like Hasmah in being visibly supportive without wanting or enjoying equal billing.
But it was easier for Kwa because she did not have to constantly accompany her husband in his public role as Hasmah had to in respect of Mahathir.
She was busy running a law firm that supported her family — “I am a kept man”, as Lee wryly remarked — and so she had a reason not to be constantly at her husband’s side.
Hasmah was a great help to her husband on public occasions that required an expression of grief and sympathy.

Her evident but understated sorrow, expressed in sympathy visits following tragedies such as the collapse of Highlands Towers in 1993 and the fire at Bright Sparklers that killed several people, as well as visits to the widows of Cabinet ministers such as Chan Siang Sun, was unfeigned and moving.
One thing that was intriguing about Hasmah was the frequency with which she appeared in public without a headscarf. Yet, there was hardly a qualm about her rectitude as a Muslim woman.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
